lesson_title: Ethereum - Accounts, the EVM and Transactions

metadata.note: The lesson names no assigned reading. Reading questions rest on documents the lesson cites (Wood, Ellis et al. and Eskandari et al., Flashbots, Otterscan) and each states a fact that is on a visible slide. Only the visible slides count; the hidden slides get no questions. Coverage: one question for each visible check, worked, practice, answers and review slide, plus the balances, contract, transaction, receipt and internal-transfer slides.

lectures.title: Ethereum - Accounts, the EVM and Transactions - lesson synthesis
Ethereum - Accounts, the EVM and Transactions - reading synthesis

questions.question_stem: Block 3's transaction is from Account 1, whose address page shows a balance and a nonce but no Contract tab. What kind of account sent it, and what evidence says so?
questions.correct_answer: An EOA: only an EOA can start a transaction, and an address with no code shows no Contract tab.
incorrect_answers: A contract account: it holds a balance and a nonce, and a contract can start a transaction by its code.
An EOA, because the explorer prints an [EOA] tag beside the address, and that tag settles it alone.
A contract account, because only an account with code has a nonce, which shows it ran a program.
questions.explanation: Two pieces of evidence, of different kinds: only an EOA can start a transaction, and an address with no code has no Contract tab. The explorer's [EOA] tag is a label to check against the code.
questions.lesson_block: Check: block 3. Which account type sent it?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Check: block 3. Which account type sent it?

questions.question_stem: On Ethereum's main network, a payment sits in a block made two minutes ago. The agent asks: "So it's done, and can't be undone?" What do you answer?
questions.correct_answer: Not yet: it is included, not final, and becomes final about 15 minutes after the block, once validators holding two-thirds of staked ETH vote for a later checkpoint.
incorrect_answers: Yes: it is in a block, and a payment is final once a validator has put it in a block and every node has re-run it, so nothing more is needed to settle it.
Not yet: it is included, and becomes final once six or more later blocks sit on top of it, about as many as Bitcoin needs for a payment to settle fully.
Yes: every node has rerun it in the EVM and recorded the same result, and that agreement of every node is what makes a payment final and permanent on Ethereum.
questions.explanation: Included is not final. The block becomes final once validators holding two-thirds of staked ETH vote for a later checkpoint, about 15 minutes after the block. More blocks on top do not make it final; the votes do.
questions.lesson_block: Check: a block two minutes old. Final?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Check: a block two minutes old. Final?

questions.question_stem: Block 3 paid a fee of 0.000016180715292 ETH for 21,000 gas. Under EIP-1559, how is that fee split?
questions.correct_answer: Nearly all of it is burned as the base fee, and 21,000 wei, the tip, goes to the block's fee recipient.
incorrect_answers: All of it goes to the validator who proposed the block, as the network's reward for the work done.
Half of it is burned and half goes to the fee recipient, because the base fee and tip are equal parts.
The base fee goes to the fee recipient and the tip is burned, which limits the transaction count.
questions.explanation: Under EIP-1559 the base fee is destroyed and the tip goes to the block's fee recipient. Block 3: 16,180.715271 Gwei burned, 21,000 wei tip, 0.000016180715292 ETH in all.
questions.lesson_block: Worked: block 3's fee, most of it burned
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Worked: block 3's fee, most of it burned

questions.question_stem: Block 6's transaction shows Status Fail, Value 0 ETH and no logs. What did it still cost Account 4?
questions.correct_answer: The fee for the 24,835 gas it used, and Account 4's nonce 0, which the failed transaction used up.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because a failed transaction is undone whole, so Account 4's balance and nonce stay as they were.
The fee for the whole 100,000 gas limit, because the sender pays the limit it set and not the gas used.
The fee, but nonce 0 stays free for the next try, because a failed one does not count in a sequence.
questions.explanation: A failed call still pays for the gas it used (24,835 of 100,000), and its changes are undone. Account 4's nonce 0 is used up all the same, and no log was written.
questions.lesson_block: Worked: block 6's receipt: status 0, fee paid
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Worked: block 6's receipt: status 0, fee paid

questions.question_stem: An agent read only the To field of blocks 4 and 5 and wrote: "Account 0 paid the token contract; Account 1 paid the Splitter." What do you tell the agent?
questions.correct_answer: The To field names the contract each transaction called, not who received the value; the receivers are in the logs and the internal transfers.
incorrect_answers: The To field is right for both, because the value of a transaction always ends with the account that the To field names, so report both of them.
Block 4 is right, since the token contract holds the tokens, but block 5 is wrong, since the Splitter kept none of the ETH it was sent.
The To field is empty for a contract call, so the agent should read the From field to find out who received the value of each one.
questions.explanation: The To field is the contract each transaction called. The token receiver is in the log, and the ETH a contract passes on is in the internal transfers.
questions.lesson_block: Practice: blocks 4 and 5. Who received what?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Practice: blocks 4 and 5. Who received what?

questions.question_stem: Block 4's log reads Transfer 5,000 CRT from Account 0 to Account 3. Which statement about Account 3 needs a confidence word such as High, Moderate or Low?
questions.correct_answer: That one particular person holds Account 3's key, because the chain cannot show who holds a key.
incorrect_answers: That Account 3 received 5,000 CRT, because a log is only the token contract's own report.
That the transaction carried 0 ETH, because the explorer's Value field can differ from the chain record.
That the transaction paid a fee, because the fee is a judgment the explorer works out from gas used.
questions.explanation: The chain records the log, the internal transfers and the fee, so they need no confidence word. Who holds an account's key is a judgment the chain cannot make, so it takes High, Moderate or Low.
questions.lesson_block: Answers: the logs and the internal transfer
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Answers: the logs and the internal transfer

questions.question_stem: An agent sees a contract call with Value 0 ETH and writes that nothing moved. What is the better reading?
questions.correct_answer: Not necessarily: a token moves by a contract call with `value` 0, and the receiver is found in the logs.
incorrect_answers: Nothing moved in ETH or in tokens, because a call with Value 0 ETH carries no data for a contract.
Tokens may have moved, and the receiver is found in the To field, because To names who gets tokens.
Only the fee moved, because a call to a contract never changes any account except the sender's.
questions.explanation: Question 2 of the review: a token moves by a contract call with value 0, and its receiver is in the logs, so Value 0 ETH does not mean nothing moved.
questions.lesson_block: Review: account, transaction, receipt, in order
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Review: account, transaction, receipt, in order

questions.question_stem: An analyst tries Bitcoin's change heuristic on block 3, where Account 1 paid 1.5 ETH to Account 2. Why does it have nothing to work on?
questions.correct_answer: Ethereum has no change output: the sender's balance just goes down by the value and the fee.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum returns the change to a new address, so the change cannot be tied back to the sender.
Ethereum spends outputs whole as Bitcoin does, but every explorer hides which of them is change.
Ethereum keeps balances only for contract accounts, so a sender's change is not in its balance.
questions.explanation: Ethereum keeps one record per account and edits its balance and nonce in place. There is no change output, so Bitcoin's change heuristic has nothing to work on.
questions.lesson_block: Ethereum edits balances; Bitcoin spends outputs
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Ethereum edits balances; Bitcoin spends outputs

questions.question_stem: On the lab chain, where does the token contract `0x5FbDB…` keep each holder's token balance?
questions.correct_answer: In its own storage: a token is an entry in the contract's storage, not a balance the chain keeps.
incorrect_answers: In each holder's account: a token is a balance the chain keeps, as it keeps ETH, in its fields.
In the storage root of each holder's own account, because every account has a storage root for tokens.
In the `value` field of each transaction: it carries the token amount, and the chain adds it per holder.
questions.explanation: The token contract keeps every holder's balance in its own storage. A token is an entry in that storage, not a balance the chain keeps.
questions.lesson_block: A contract is code plus storage at an address
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: A contract is code plus storage at an address

questions.question_stem: Block 4's transaction has the token contract in To and 0 ETH in `value`. Which kind of transaction is it, and where is the function named?
questions.correct_answer: A contract call, and the `data` field names a function such as `transfer(address,uint256)`.
incorrect_answers: A plain transfer, and the `value` field names the function and the token amount to send.
A contract deployment, and the `to` field holds the code that creates the token contract.
A contract call, and the `nonce` field names the function that the sender wants run.
questions.explanation: A token moves by a contract call: data names a function such as transfer(address,uint256) and value stays 0. That is why the receiver is not in the To field.
questions.lesson_block: A transaction is a signed, numbered message
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: A transaction is a signed, numbered message

questions.question_stem: In block 7, Account 3 sent a call to the token contract with Value 0 ETH, and its one log reads Transfer 250 CRT from Account 3 to Account 1. Who received the tokens?
questions.correct_answer: Account 1, because a token transfer shows up in the logs, not in `value`.
incorrect_answers: The token contract, because To names the account that receives the tokens.
Nobody, because Value was 0 ETH and a log records only an event, nothing more.
Account 3, because a log names the account that sent the call, not the receiver.
questions.explanation: A token transfer shows up in the logs, not in value. The log names Account 1 as the receiver, though To names the token contract.
questions.lesson_block: The receipt says what actually happened
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: The receipt says what actually happened

questions.question_stem: Block 5's transaction shows Account 1 sending 2 ETH to the Splitter. Where do you read that the ETH reached Accounts 2 and 4?
questions.correct_answer: In the internal transfers: ETH a contract sends during a transaction, which are not transactions of their own.
incorrect_answers: In the To and Value fields of the transaction, which list every account the contract paid during the call, in order.
In the logs, because a contract records each ETH it sends as a Transfer event in the receipt of the call.
In new transactions from the Splitter, since each ETH it sends is a separate signed transaction of its own.
questions.explanation: The transaction shows only Account 1 to the Splitter. The ETH the Splitter sent on is an internal transfer, found by a trace; it is not a transaction of its own and wrote no log.
questions.lesson_block: Contracts move value the transaction won't show
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Contracts move value the transaction won't show

questions.question_stem: A developer wants a contract to fetch an asset's price from a website while it runs. Why can't an EVM contract do that?
questions.correct_answer: To stay deterministic, a contract sees only the transaction's data and defined block fields, so every node gets the same result.
incorrect_answers: Gas meters every operation, and a website request would cost more gas than any one transaction is allowed to hold in a block.
A contract reads outside facts only through its creator's key, which signs each website request for every node on the network.
Every node would fetch the page at the same moment, so the site would block the repeat requests and the nodes would time out and stall.
questions.explanation: Determinism requires that every node reach the same result, so a contract cannot read websites, a clock or random numbers. It sees only the transaction's data and defined block fields (Wood, 2016).
questions.lesson_block: One program on every node, seeing only the chain
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: One program on every node, seeing only the chain
questions.specific_source_reading: Wood, Ethereum Yellow Paper (`wood_ethereumsecuredecentralised_2016`): the EVM is deterministic, so every node reaches the same result from the same inputs

questions.question_stem: A contract acts on an asset's price that an oracle supplies. What does that add for the analyst to weigh?
questions.correct_answer: Trust in whoever supplies the oracle's data, because an oracle brings outside facts on chain.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because the nodes that rerun the contract also check the price against the market.
Trust in the validators, because an oracle is a validator duty and its price is voted on.
Trust in the contract's creator alone, since the code fixed the price when deployed to the chain.
questions.explanation: An oracle puts outside facts on chain and adds trust in whoever supplies them (Ellis et al., 2017; Eskandari et al., 2021).
questions.lesson_block: One program on every node, seeing only the chain
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: One program on every node, seeing only the chain
questions.specific_source_reading: Ellis, Juels and Nazarov, Chainlink (`ellis_chainlinkdecentralizedoracle_2017`) and Eskandari et al., SoK: Oracles (`eskandari_sokoraclesground_2021`): an oracle brings outside data on chain, and a contract trusts whoever supplies it

questions.question_stem: A block's tip went to an address that is not the validator who proposed the block. Which explanation does the lesson give?
questions.correct_answer: The fee recipient can be a builder, a firm that assembles blocks and pays the proposer to use them.
incorrect_answers: The fee recipient is the miner of the previous block, because tips are paid one block late.
The tip is burned with the base fee, so that address is a burn address and not an account.
The sender names the fee recipient in a transaction field, so any address can be given the tip by it.
questions.explanation: The fee recipient can be a builder, a firm that assembles blocks and pays the proposer to use them (Flashbots builder payments).
questions.lesson_block: Worked: block 3's fee, most of it burned
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Worked: block 3's fee, most of it burned
questions.specific_source_reading: Flashbots, builder payments (`flashbots_builderpayments_2026`): a builder assembles a block and pays the proposer, and can be the fee recipient

questions.question_stem: How does Otterscan find the ETH a contract sends on during a transaction, such as the Splitter's 1 ETH to Account 2?
questions.correct_answer: It asks the node to replay the transaction step by step, a trace, and lists the internal transfers.
incorrect_answers: It reads the receipt's logs, where the Splitter wrote each send as an event with its topics.
It reads the transaction's data field, which holds a signed list of every account the contract will pay.
It reads the validators' votes for the block, which record each send made while the block ran.
questions.explanation: Otterscan asks the node to replay the transaction step by step, a trace, and lists the internal transfers (Otterscan ots namespace).
questions.lesson_block: Contracts move value the transaction won't show
questions.specific_source_lesson: 01-EF-ethereum_intro.qmd: Contracts move value the transaction won't show
questions.specific_source_reading: Otterscan, ots namespace (`otterscan_otsnamespace_2026`): the node's trace shows internal calls that send ETH, which a transaction alone does not show
